title: We Need to Talk About 504-Maxxing
author: Tim Daly
summary: Tim Daly examines why access to school accommodations has become tied to family wealth. After the College Board made it easier in 2017 for students with 504 plans to get the same exam accommodations, a Princeton study found 504 plans rose faster in affluent communities, and other research shows IEPs are concentrated among poorer children while 504s skew wealthy. District administrators describe privileged parents arriving with a clinician's letter, a contagion effect among families, and accommodations such as multi-day testing or phone access that staff feel unable to refuse. At colleges the shift is steeper, with the share of students registered with disability offices reaching 19 percent at Harvard and 38 percent at Stanford, concentrated at selective schools. Daly stresses that he is not criticising families or claiming any designations are wrong, and offers possibilities such as evaluating poorer students better or offering supports like extended time to everyone. His warning is that accommodations should provide supports, not advantages, and a backlash could make it harder for students who truly need them.
points: A 2017 College Board change that eased exam accommodations for 504 students was followed by a disproportionate rise in plans in affluent communities.
IEPs are more common among low-income students while 504 plans skew toward higher-income students, even within the same school.
Administrators say they struggle to resist requests, including for unlimited breaks or phone access, because families escalate to district leaders and boards.
Disability registration at elite colleges has jumped, from three percent at Harvard in 2014 to 19 percent in 2024, with very high rates almost exclusively at selective schools.
Daly argues schools should consider universal supports and better evaluation for poorer families so accommodations do not become a first-class cabin.
quotes: The College Board’s change was sensible and fair. Students still had to request approval, but they no longer had to demonstrate their need for accommodations from scratch.
Affluence has become strongly predictive of whether a student will receive a 504 plan rather than an IEP.
I spoke with the director of student services in a large district who explained that privileged parents often show up to her schools with a clinician’s letter already in hand.
They described something like a social contagion among families who hear about accommodations other students are receiving and then seek them for their own children.
The administrators feel unable to push back, even when they see accommodations as excessive or unnecessary, because families will press their case to senior district leaders or board members.
Rates are up broadly. In 2008, not a single college on the list had 20+ percent of its students registered with a disability. In 2017, three did. By 2024, 23 of them did.
Maybe there are useful supports we should just offer all students, regardless of disability status, like extended time.
Accommodations should provide educational supports, not advantages. If we allow them to be stretched beyond their proper use and original intent, suspicion will grow.
